body: @piuccio If Rollup thinks that `Something` is free of side-effects, it'll tree-shake the call. So long as you're doing [something side-effectful](http://rollupjs.org/#%7B%22options%22%3A%7B%22format%22%3A%22iife%22%2C%22moduleName%22%3A%22myBundle%22%2C%22globals%22%3A%7B%7D%7D%2C%22modules%22%3A%5B%7B%22name%22%3A%22main.js%22%2C%22code%22%3A%22import%20%7B%20Something%20%7D%20from%20'.%2Flib'%5Cn%5CnSomething%28%29%3B%22%7D%2C%7B%22name%22%3A%22lib.js%22%2C%22code%22%3A%22export%20function%20Something%20%28%29%20%7B%5Cn%20%20%2F%2F%20do%20some%20magic%20in%20the%20brower%5Cn%20%20%2F%2F%20uncomment%20this%20line%3A%5Cn%20%20%2F%2F%20window.foo%20%3D%201%3B%5Cn%7D%22%7D%5D%7D) you should be fine. If you think Rollup mistakenly considers something side-effectful to be pure, please try to distill a minimal reproducing example.

@Victorystick, where are side effects identified in the source code? I can take a look at this.

Rollup should recognize that `document` is not a global variable, and accessing any variables not controlled by Rollup can have a side effect.

issue.title: function with for...in or for...of removed during tree-shaking

body:
**My situation:** I want to bundle SVG icons into my Angular2 app's JS
1. I use `gulp-plugin-string` to make the SVG icons globals in my entry file
2. I transform the global string variable to an SVG element in the Angular2 code

However, rollup tree-shakes the global as it thinks I never use it. I can't import it in the actual angular code because `ngc` can't understand the special SVG import.

How do I get rollup to not tree-shake the result of `gulp-plugin-string`, and keep it as a global variable?
Ok, I figured out if I add the imported SVGs to `window` then all is good...

issue.title: [WIP] account for side-effects in call expression arguments, and functions passed to functions

body: Here's a [super minimal example](http://rollupjs.org/?version=0.41.1&) where Rollup thinks `Promise` is a pure function.
@Rich-Harris Any thoughts on the patch above? I think it's correct.

It's correct insofar as it fixes this case, but strictly speaking `Promise` and its methods *don't* have side-effects, it's just that their arguments might. For example this...

```js
var x = Promise.resolve( 42 );
```

...unambiguously *doesn't* have side-effects. What we really need to do is account for side-effects in arguments, in particular by assuming that function arguments are called. #1207 was an attempt in that direction but it had false positives.

I'm doing some experimentation at the moment into whether it's possible to get more accurate results by simulating what would actually happen if the code was run, and only bailing out when that gets too hard. Bear with me...

> strictly speaking Promise and its methods don't have side-effects, it's just that their arguments might.

But the argument to the Promise constructor is not a function call - it's a function expression.

A function expression (or arrow expression) is always side effect free - unless it is invoked. But in the case of the Promise constructor - the argument function expression is always guaranteed to be called, and as result can potentially have side effects.

If your rewrite involves special-casing the Promise constructor, sure, that can work.

@Rich-Harris Could we at least make the behavior configurable in the meantime? I'd rather make it a bit more conservative.

Also, I don't really understand why you'd want to strip out `new Promise(fn)` in particular. Can you give an example of a promise constructor that doesn't have any side effects?
Oh, wow, @kzc just made the exact same point. Sorry about the noise.
